days.title: AIP Logic Building Blocks: Typed Outputs, Prompts, Tools and Blocks

concepts.heading: What an AIP Logic Function Is
concepts.body: AIP Logic is the no-code way to build an LLM-powered function in Foundry. A Logic function has typed inputs and typed outputs, a prompt with variables injected from those inputs, and blocks that can call tools, branch or loop. Once published, the function can be called from Workshop applications, Actions and automations like any other function. Because it can also make Ontology edits, its output can change real objects, which is why the exam treats Logic design as engineering rather than prompt writing.

concepts.heading: Typed Outputs Instead of Text to Parse
concepts.body: Consumers of a Logic function, such as an automation that branches on a decision, should receive a structure and not free text they have to parse. Declare decision-style values as enumerations, numbers as numbers and flags as booleans, grouped in a struct when several values travel together. A collection should be a typed list of records with validated references, for example a capped list of article ids with a reason each, rather than a comma-separated string. Making 'not found' an explicit typed field, such as a boolean next to the answer and its citation, turns a grounded refusal into something you can test.

concepts.heading: Variables and Context: Inject What the Task Needs
concepts.body: Prompt behaviour should be driven by the function's inputs through variable injection, for example injecting a customer's preferred language property and returning that language in the typed output so it can be checked. Context from the Ontology is fetched inside the function: traverse links from the input object or use an Ontology query tool scoped to that object, then inject the results. For long documents, retrieve only the relevant chunks with semantic search instead of pasting the whole document into the prompt. Optional inputs should be modelled as optional and handled explicitly, with conditionals or a clear 'not provided' value, and tested with and without them.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between a Single Completion, Conditionals, Loops and Tools
concepts.body: Use the simplest block that does the job. A single completion with no tools is faster, cheaper and more predictable when all the information is already in the inputs. Fixed rules, such as routing claims above an amount threshold or routing long documents by a measured page or token count, belong in a conditional block on a typed value, not in a model judgement. A loop block suits a list of independent items, running one bounded completion per item and collecting a list output. Tool-using reasoning is justified only when the model must decide from the input which lookups to make and then use their results.

concepts.heading: Making Tool Use Safe and Bounded
concepts.body: When a function does use tools, give each tool a clear description so the model knows when it applies. Reuse existing published functions as tools instead of re-implementing their logic inside a prompt, and inject their typed results as variables. Live facts such as a current rate should come from a function or an Ontology object kept current by a sync, with any arithmetic done in code and only the result handed to the model to phrase. Tool-using loops need explicit stop rules, an iteration cap and a defined fallback output so a run cannot wander indefinitely.

examPoints: When a scenario has a downstream automation or app parsing the model's text, prefer a typed output (enumeration, number, boolean or struct) so consumers branch on fields and invalid values cannot leave the function.

When a scenario offers tool-using reasoning for a task whose data is already in the inputs, or a model judgement for a fixed numeric rule, prefer a single completion or a conditional block on the typed value.

quiz.q: A Logic function must produce a risk note for each line item of an order, and the items are independent of each other. Which design fits best?
choices: One completion that receives the whole order and returns all notes as a single block of text for the app to split
A loop block over the typed list of line items, running one bounded completion per item and collecting a list output
A tool-using reasoning block that lets the model decide on its own how many items to look at before answering
A conditional block that sends orders with many items to a larger model and short orders to a smaller one
quiz.explain: Independent items in a typed list are handled with a loop block, one bounded completion each, which keeps every run small and the output typed; one big text answer must be parsed, and open-ended tool reasoning adds cost and unpredictability.

quiz.q: A function's answer depends on today's exchange rate and a calculation using it. What is the most reliable design?
choices: Ask the model to recall a recent exchange rate and perform the calculation itself inside the completion
Paste a rate table from last quarter into the system prompt and instruct the model to use the nearest value
Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible rates before it settles on a final calculation
Fetch the current rate from a function or a synced Ontology object, compute in code, and give the model the result to phrase
quiz.explain: Live facts should come from a tool or synced object and arithmetic belongs in deterministic code; the model's memory is stale and unreliable for numbers, and temperature only adds randomness.

days.recap: Build AIP Logic functions with typed inputs and outputs, inject only the context the task needs, and use the simplest block (completion, conditional, loop, then tools) that meets the requirement.

days.title: Ontology Edits, Logic Versus Code, Traces and Versions

concepts.heading: Logic Versus Code: Where Each Belongs
concepts.body: AIP Logic is for tasks that need language understanding or interpretation. Work that is fully deterministic, needs exact arithmetic, or runs as a large scheduled batch belongs in code, as a transform or function in a Code Repository. Inside one function you can mix both: compute rule-driven values such as an SLA breach flag or a priority from a governed matrix in code, and use the model only for the bounded language part, such as urgency from free text or a written justification. A practical pattern is to match deterministically first, for example against an approved clause library after normalization, and send only the unmatched residual to a completion.

concepts.heading: Safe Ontology Edits from AI Output
concepts.body: Before a function edits an object, it should read the object's current state and apply only allowed transitions, sending conflicts to review. References the model proposes, such as an owner or reviewer, must be validated against real Ontology state; better still, present real candidates from a lookup and type the output as an object reference rather than a free-text name. Items extracted by a model should pass a validation step before objects are created, with invalid items reported rather than silently dropped. Edits should be idempotent, expressed as absolute state such as a count of linked records instead of a relative increment that doubles on a retry.

concepts.heading: Action Validation Is a Signal, Not an Obstacle
concepts.body: When an Action rejects values produced by a Logic function, the Action is doing its job. The right response is to inspect the rejections, fix the function's output so it satisfies the constraints, and add the failing cases to the evaluation suite. Weakening the Action's validation to let AI output through removes the last guard on the data. Before enabling writes at all, test edit-producing functions on a few sample inputs with edits disabled or on a branch, review the proposed edits, then enable them with a bounded first run.

concepts.heading: Debugging with Execution Traces
concepts.body: Each Logic run leaves a trace: the resolved prompt after variables were injected, every tool call with its result, the raw model response and the parsed output. Walk the trace in that order to find the failing stage instead of guessing. If the resolved prompt still contains a literal placeholder, a variable binding failed, usually through a typo or a renamed variable, and a check for unresolved placeholders prevents a repeat. When behaviour changes after an edit or a model change, compare traces of failing cases against the last good version, and turn the stored inputs of incident runs into evaluation cases.

concepts.heading: Publishing Versions and Migrating Consumers
concepts.body: Applications and automations call a published version of a function. Publish changes as a new version, evaluate it against the suite and inspect traces for a sample of cases, then move each consumer deliberately while the previous version stays available. New required inputs can be introduced as optional with a default first, with consumers migrated in sequence. A gradual rollout can route a share of calls to the new version and compare per-version metrics. When prompt variants or structures score the same within measured variance, choose the cheaper and simpler one, such as a single completion over a chain, and record the evidence.

examPoints: When a scenario shows a published function misbehaving right after a prompt edit, prefer comparing traces against the previous version while consumers stay on that version, rather than a bigger model, a higher temperature or a rewrite.
When a scenario describes exact, repeatable rules or a large scheduled computation, prefer deterministic code and reserve the model for the part that needs language.

quiz.q: An Action keeps rejecting values written by an AI function because they fall outside an allowed range. What should the AI engineer do?
choices: Inspect the rejected cases, fix the function's output to meet the constraints, and add those cases to the evaluation suite
Relax the Action's validation rules so the AI-generated values can be written without further rejections
Switch the function to a larger model and republish it immediately so every consumer receives the change
Remove the Action and let the function write the property directly so validation no longer blocks the workflow
quiz.explain: Action validation failures show the function's output is wrong; fixing the output and capturing the cases keeps the guard in place, while weakening or bypassing validation lets bad data through.

quiz.q: A trace shows the resolved prompt still contains a literal placeholder where the customer's name should be. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model's temperature was set too low, so it repeated the template text instead of filling it in
The model's context window is too small, so the variable value was cut off before the prompt was sent
The variable was not bound, for example through a typo or a renamed variable, so injection never happened
The published version is cached by consumers, so the latest prompt text has not yet reached the model
quiz.explain: A literal placeholder in the resolved prompt means the variable binding failed; fix the name and add a check for unresolved placeholders. The other options would not leave the template text in the resolved prompt.

days.recap: Keep exact rules in code and language in the model, validate before every Ontology edit, debug by walking traces, and ship changes as evaluated versions that consumers move to deliberately.

days.title: Agent Types, Deployment Channels and Agent Context

concepts.heading: Standard Agents Versus AIP Assist
concepts.body: AIP Agent Studio is where standard agents are designed: purpose-built assistants with their own instructions, retrieval context, tools and model. AIP Assist is the platform-wide helper that answers questions about using Foundry itself. A business assistant, such as one that answers questions about suppliers or shipments, should be built as a standard agent and not expected from AIP Assist. Instructions, tools and retrieval are configured and tried interactively in Agent Studio before deployment, and the test conversations used there become the start of an evaluation suite.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Deployment Channel
concepts.body: An agent embedded in a Workshop module can use the module's application state, such as the selected object, and the module's Actions, so users stay where they work. A standalone agent suits a general assistant that needs no application context, such as a company-wide process helper. One agent can be deployed through both channels with shared instructions and retrieval, as long as its tools tolerate missing application state. When questions span several specialist agents, a coordinating agent that routes and combines answers is preferred over merging everything into one large agent.

concepts.heading: Passing Application State
concepts.body: Embedding is useful because the agent knows what the user is looking at. Pass the selected object as application state so the agent's prompts and tools apply to that object, and scope tools and retrieval to it, for example to the selected machine or purchase order. Application state can also drive an opening behaviour, where the agent calls a function on the selected customer when the session starts and presents a summary before the user asks. When adding a new channel, check how identity maps to the platform, what context the channel provides and how output renders, and evaluate the agent for that channel.

concepts.heading: Retrieval Context for Agents
concepts.body: Agents over a large knowledge base should assemble context per turn through retrieval, not through a static dump of every document in the instructions. Retrieve only the object types and documentation relevant to the question, rank deterministically, remove overlaps, label sources and instruct the agent to synthesize across them. Retrieval and tools must run with the user's permissions so the agent can only reach what that user is allowed to see. Authorization is never left to the prompt or to filtering the answer afterwards.

concepts.heading: Conversation State
concepts.body: Within a session, follow-up turns should use the earlier messages so the user does not repeat context. Session history should never be shared across users. If conversations surface knowledge that should improve the agent, it goes into the corpus only through a reviewed process, not by letting one user's session influence another's. Clear instructions on when to ask a single targeted clarifying question and when to proceed with a stated assumption keep multi-turn conversations efficient, and both paths should be tested.

examPoints: When a scenario needs an assistant that works with the objects and Actions of a specific app, prefer a standard agent built in AIP Agent Studio and embedded in that Workshop module with the selection passed as application state.
When a scenario proposes AIP Assist for a business-specific task, prefer a standard agent; AIP Assist remains the helper for using the platform itself.

quiz.q: A company wants an assistant that answers general HR process questions from anywhere, with no link to a particular application. Which deployment fits?
choices: An agent embedded in every Workshop module so it can read whichever object the user has selected
AIP Assist configured with the HR documents so it answers process questions alongside platform help
A standalone standard agent with retrieval over the HR process documentation
A Logic function triggered by an automation each time an employee record is updated
quiz.explain: An assistant that needs no application context is deployed standalone; embedding adds nothing without app state, AIP Assist is the platform helper, and an automation does not answer user questions.

quiz.q: An embedded maintenance agent should answer questions about the machine a technician has just tapped in the app. How does the agent know which machine is meant?
choices: The technician types the machine's serial number at the start of every conversation
The selected machine is passed to the agent as application state and its tools are scoped to that machine
The agent searches all machines by name and picks the one whose description best matches the question
The instructions list every machine in the plant so the model can infer which one is meant
quiz.explain: Embedding lets the module pass the user's selection as state, so prompts and tools apply to that object; name matching and static lists are error-prone and do not scale.

days.recap: Build business agents as standard agents in AIP Agent Studio, embed them where the work happens with the selection passed as state, deploy standalone when no app context is needed, and retrieve context per turn under the user's permissions.

days.title: Agent Tools, Guardrails, Escalation and Release Testing

concepts.heading: Least-Privilege Tools
concepts.body: Give an agent only the narrow tools its task needs, read-only wherever possible. A requirement that an agent must never do something, such as place orders, is enforced by not giving it any tool or Action that can do it, not by an instruction. Tools and safeguards scale with consequence: a question-answering agent gets read-only retrieval, while an agent that issues refunds gets a controlled Action with validation, limits, idempotency, audit and restricted invocation. State-changing tool calls should show the user a preview and require confirmation, while read tools stay frictionless.

concepts.heading: Guiding Tool Selection and Answer Shape
concepts.body: Agents choose tools from their descriptions and instructions, so precise descriptions that say when a tool applies are the first fix when a tool is called too often or too rarely. Answer format and scope are shaped by instructions, with examples for tone, and are measured in the evaluation suite. For constrained displays, a typed output such as a list capped at a few short strings is more reliable than asking for brevity in prose. Cutting retrieval context or truncating answers to fix format usually harms accuracy instead.

concepts.heading: Guardrails as Tested Behaviour
concepts.body: Every grounded agent needs a tested path for 'the evidence does not answer this', where it says it cannot answer instead of guessing. A topic boundary, such as no legal advice, is defined in the instructions, backed by an output check and covered by paraphrased adversarial cases, not by a list of banned phrases. Content the agent must not use is removed or filtered out of retrieval and paired with refusal behaviour that refers the user to the right people. Out-of-scope requests should be recognized and redirected, and their frequency monitored to plan future scope.

concepts.heading: Designing Escalation
concepts.body: Escalation needs explicit triggers that the agent recognizes, a summary of the conversation so far, and a handoff into a ticket or queue that carries that summary. The user should get clear next steps rather than a dead end. Repeated user requests for a capability the agent lacks are a product signal: quantify them, decide whether the capability is appropriate, and add it with controls or improve the redirect. Escalation paths are part of what is tested before release.

concepts.heading: Testing and Releasing an Agent
concepts.body: Before release, test typical, edge, insufficient-evidence, unauthorized and adversarial conversations, with extra focus on tools that change data. Derive adversarial cases from the agent's actual tools and data, such as attempts to reach documents outside the user's permissions, instructions hidden in documents and requests to fabricate citations. Test as several identities with different permissions and assert what each can see. Release in stages, starting with a pilot of representative users, keep the pilot cases as a regression suite, watch traces and feedback, and set rollback criteria in advance. An untested capability is never added to a validated release at the last minute.

examPoints: When a scenario states that an agent must never perform an operation, prefer withholding the tool or Action that performs it over stronger wording in the instructions.

When a scenario asks how to prepare an agent for wider release, prefer evaluation across typical, edge, unauthorized and adversarial cases plus a staged pilot with rollback criteria over a single broad launch.

quiz.q: A grounded policy agent sometimes invents answers to questions the policy documents do not cover. What is the best first fix?
choices: Add more documents to the retrieval context so that every possible question has some text to draw on
Switch the agent to the largest available model so it reasons more carefully about missing information
Remove retrieval and rely on the model's general knowledge, which covers a wider range of questions
Instruct the agent to say it cannot answer when retrieved context gives no support, and test that path with out-of-scope questions
quiz.explain: A grounded agent needs an explicit, tested 'not supported by the evidence' path; more context, bigger models or dropping retrieval do not stop guessing and often make it worse.

quiz.q: An agent can both look up order status and create return requests. Which confirmation design is most appropriate?
choices: Confirmation with a preview of what will be created for the return tool, and none for the read-only lookup
Confirmation for every tool call, including status lookups, so that users approve each step the agent takes
No confirmation for either tool, relying on instructions telling the agent to create returns only when needed
A daily report of created returns for a supervisor to read, with no confirmation inside the conversation
quiz.explain: State-changing calls get a confirmation that shows what will happen, while read tools stay frictionless; confirming everything adds friction, and instructions or later reports do not prevent a wrong write.

days.recap: Give agents the fewest, safest tools, enforce 'never' by withholding capability, make refusal and escalation tested behaviours, and release through evaluation, a pilot and rollback criteria.

days.title: Chunking, Metadata and Embeddings for Retrieval

concepts.heading: How Semantic Search Works
concepts.body: An embedding model turns text into a vector so that similar meanings land close together. At indexing time every chunk is embedded and stored, for example as a vector property on a chunk object in the Ontology. At query time the question is embedded with the same model and the nearest chunk vectors are returned. Each embedding model has its own vector space, so the embedding model is effectively part of the index: changing it means re-embedding the corpus before queries switch, and the choice of model is made by measuring retrieval quality.

concepts.heading: Chunking Strategy
concepts.body: Long documents are split into self-contained chunks so that retrieval returns the passage that actually holds the answer. Chunks should follow section boundaries and keep their section heading, and a modest overlap helps when answers span a boundary, while large overlaps mostly add near-duplicates. Chunking should be consistent across the corpus, because mixed chunk sizes distort similarity ranking, with short chunks matching queries more tightly. Tables are chunked by row or small row groups with the header row and sheet title attached, so each chunk describes itself.

concepts.heading: Metadata on Every Chunk
concepts.body: Store metadata with each chunk that enables filtering, freshness and citations: a document identifier, title, section, version and effective date, and fields such as country, product, division or document type. A stable identifier and location carried into the context is what makes verifiable citations possible later. Document-type metadata lets you rank FAQ entries and long manuals sensibly instead of letting one type drown the other. Language metadata, together with a multilingual embedding model, supports corpora that mix languages in one vector space.

concepts.heading: Building the Corpus as a Pipeline
concepts.body: A retrieval corpus is maintained data, built by a pipeline in the pipeline layer. The stages are: extract text, chunk by section with metadata, embed with the model that queries will use, and write chunk objects with vector properties. The pipeline runs incrementally, re-chunking and re-embedding only changed documents and removing superseded chunks. Visual content such as drawings can be indexed by generating structured descriptions with a vision model in the pipeline and embedding those descriptions.

concepts.heading: Structured Facts Are Not a Search Problem
concepts.body: Not everything belongs in a vector index. Tabular reference data such as a price list should stay as structured objects with exact lookup by identifier, and a machine's structured properties are read directly from its object. Semantic search is for unstructured text such as manuals and procedures. A good design combines both: free-text evidence from semantic search and structured facts from the object, assembled into one context. Chunk objects should also carry their source document's permissions so retrieval executed as the user returns only authorized chunks.

examPoints: When a scenario shows retrieval quality collapsing after an embedding model upgrade, prefer re-embedding the corpus with the new model (or reverting queries) because query and chunk vectors must come from the same model.
When a scenario asks for exact facts such as prices or part attributes, prefer an exact lookup on structured objects over adding the table to the semantic index.

quiz.q: A team indexes a policy library and wants answers to cite the exact section and version they came from. What must be in place at indexing time?
choices: A larger embedding model so that each chunk vector carries enough detail to identify its source
Each chunk stored with a stable document identifier and its title, section and version as metadata
A system prompt telling the model to name the section and version it believes the answer came from
Chunks as large as possible so that every chunk contains the whole document's title page
quiz.explain: Verifiable citations need chunk-level provenance captured at indexing and carried into the context; a model cannot reliably remember sources, and bigger vectors or chunks do not add identifiers.

quiz.q: A retrieval index was built from documents chunked three different ways over time, and short chunks now dominate the results. What is the best fix?
choices: Increase the number of retrieved chunks so that longer chunks also have a chance to appear
Instruct the model to prefer longer passages when it writes the answer from the retrieved text
Switch to a larger generation model that can tell relevant long passages from short ones
Re-chunk the whole corpus with one consistent strategy and re-evaluate retrieval quality
quiz.explain: Inconsistent chunk sizes skew similarity because short chunks match queries more tightly; one consistent chunking strategy fixes the ranking, while retrieving more or changing the generator does not.

days.recap: Chunk consistently along sections with rich metadata, embed queries and chunks with the same model, maintain the corpus with an incremental pipeline, and keep exact facts as structured lookups.

days.title: Retrieval Precision, Freshness, Token Budgets and Grounding Diagnosis

concepts.heading: Precision Before Volume
concepts.body: Retrieving more chunks rarely improves answers; more context often means more noise or conflicting evidence. Improve retrieval with metadata filters, a relevance threshold or drop-off rule that excludes weak chunks, and reranking. When the right chunk is retrieved but ranked low, add a reranking stage over a candidate set rather than injecting more. Applying metadata filters before similarity search also shrinks the candidate set enough to afford reranking. Rerankers have a cost, so tune the number of candidates and the reranker size while measuring both quality and latency.

concepts.heading: Freshness and Approval Through Filters
concepts.body: Freshness is a retrieval problem before it is a prompt problem. Keep status, version and effective-date metadata on chunks, filter default retrieval to current content, and offer an explicit 'as of date' mode for historical questions. Unapproved drafts are excluded from the corpus or filtered on an approval-status field enforced by the pipeline; the model is never trusted to tell drafts apart. Recency should be used to exclude superseded content rather than to boost ranking, because boosting can crowd out older but still valid material. When answers cite outdated text, first check whether superseded chunks are still indexed.

concepts.heading: Order of Operations and the Token Budget
concepts.body: Apply permissions and approval status as filters before ranking, so unauthorized or unapproved chunks are never candidates and cannot influence the answer. Then rank by similarity, rerank, and finally fit the result into the context budget. Treat context as a per-request token budget shared by a compact prompt, summarized or windowed conversation history and thresholded chunks, and validate the allocation by evaluation. One governed index can serve several assistants, each with its own filters, thresholds and rerankers applied at query time.

concepts.heading: When Queries and Documents Use Different Words
concepts.body: Identifiers, codes and part numbers embed poorly when the documents use plain names. Route queries that match an identifier pattern to an exact Ontology lookup, use hybrid retrieval that combines keyword matching with semantic search, or add a code-to-name mapping through query expansion or metadata. Ambiguous vocabulary across divisions is resolved with metadata filters driven by the user's context, with a clarifying question for users who span divisions. Compositional questions can be decomposed into sub-queries, each retrieved separately, with the evidence deduplicated and labelled.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Poorly Grounded Answers
concepts.body: Measure retrieval and generation separately. A retrieval evaluation set with labelled relevant chunks gives hit rate at k, reciprocal rank and precision directly against the index. If retrieval is good but answers are bad, fix context assembly and the prompt; if citations are right but figures are wrong, generation is blending other sources, so require verbatim figures and value checks. If recall rose but answers got worse, the context became noisier and precision needs work. In production, monitor top-score distributions, no-hit rates and sampled groundedness, and re-run the retrieval evaluation on changes.

examPoints: When a scenario shows the correct passage retrieved but ranked too low to be used, prefer adding or tuning reranking and thresholds over passing more chunks to the model.
When a scenario involves permissions or approval status in retrieval, prefer filters applied before ranking under the user's identity rather than instructions to ignore certain documents.

quiz.q: Users search with internal part codes, but the manuals refer to parts by name, so semantic search returns poor matches for code queries. What is the best fix?
choices: Route code-shaped queries to an exact lookup or add hybrid keyword retrieval or a code-to-name mapping
Increase the number of retrieved chunks so that the matching manual section eventually appears
Ask users to describe the part in words instead of typing its code into the assistant
Replace the embedding model with a larger one and keep the existing chunks as they are
quiz.explain: When queries use vocabulary the documents lack, fix retrieval with exact lookup, hybrid search or expansion; more chunks add noise, pushing work to users is not a fix, and a new embedding model without re-embedding breaks the index.

quiz.q: Retrieval tests show the right chunks are found, yet answers still ignore them. Where should the engineer look next?
choices: At the chunking pipeline, re-splitting every document into smaller chunks before anything else
At the embedding model, replacing it and re-embedding the whole corpus to improve similarity
At context assembly and the prompt, checking how chunks are presented and whether the model is told to use them
At the user permissions, widening access so the agent can retrieve a broader set of documents
quiz.explain: With retrieval measured as good, the failure is in generation: how evidence is presented and instructed. Re-chunking or re-embedding targets a stage that already works, and widening access is never a quality fix.

days.recap: Raise precision with filters, thresholds and reranking, enforce freshness, approval and permissions as filters before ranking, budget tokens deliberately, and diagnose retrieval and generation separately.

days.title: Batch LLM and Vision Processing with Structured Output

concepts.heading: Batch AI Processing in Pipelines
concepts.body: Batch LLM processing, entity extraction, visual document processing and structured output are the core data-processing capabilities this domain covers. A pipeline step sends each record or page to a model and writes the parsed result as columns. Pipeline Builder suits simpler batch AI jobs, while a Code Repositories transform is chosen when custom control such as retries, rate limiting or per-row audit is required. Every batch AI step should be designed with structured output, validation and a review path from the start, because errors at scale are written to every downstream consumer.

concepts.heading: Structured Output Schemas
concepts.body: When AI output feeds columns, ask for a typed structure and validate it before writing. Constrain categorical answers to an enumeration of the allowed values and route anything that does not match to review rather than guessing. Items that can carry several labels need a validated list of allowed values that may be empty. Several fields per document, such as parties as a list, a date as a date and a boolean flag, are extracted with one structured schema, ideally with an evidence field quoting the supporting text; adding a new field means extending the schema rather than adding a second pass.

concepts.heading: Vision-Capable Models for Images and Scans
concepts.body: Scanned or photographed documents often have no reliable text layer, so a vision-capable model reads the page image directly with a structured output schema. The same approach classifies images at scale, for example damaged, not damaged or unclear, with unclear results routed to review. Handwritten content benefits from confidence-based review of low-confidence values. A practical design routes by input type: PDFs with a good text layer go to a text model and scans go to a vision model, with each path evaluated separately.

concepts.heading: Validation Beyond Shape
concepts.body: A value can have the right type and still be wrong. Add content validation such as arithmetic checks (quantity times price against the total), language detection on translated output, and cross-checks against another source for high-consequence fields. Entity names extracted by the model are resolved deterministically after extraction, mapping variants to a canonical identifier. Inputs also need validation: a correct model applied to template or system text still produces a wrong metric, so filter inputs to the content you intend to process.

concepts.heading: Documents Larger Than the Context Window and Production Gaps
concepts.body: Documents too large for one call are processed by chunked extraction, pulling candidate fields per chunk with structured output and merging them per document with deterministic rules that flag conflicts. When production rates differ sharply from evaluation rates, the inputs differ: sample the affected rows, compare their traits with the suite, and update both the suite and the prompt. Evaluation should be weighted by the production mix and measured per type, so the segment where errors concentrate is visible. When one language fails, check text extraction, prompt assumptions and model capability in turn.

examPoints: When a scenario involves scanned or photographed pages with no reliable text, prefer a vision-capable model step with a structured output schema and validation over text-only prompts or manual entry.
When a scenario has AI output written into columns or categories, prefer an enumerated or typed schema with validation that routes failures to review over free text that is cleaned up later.

quiz.q: A pipeline extracts the supplier name from invoices, and the same supplier appears under several spellings. What is the best design?
choices: Ask the model in the extraction prompt to always spell supplier names the same way across all invoices
Keep extraction in the model and add a deterministic normalization and entity-resolution step mapping variants to a canonical id
Run the extraction twice with different temperatures and keep whichever spelling appears more often
Let analysts fix the spellings in each downstream report whenever a duplicate supplier is noticed
quiz.explain: Entity resolution is an exact, repeatable rule and belongs in deterministic code with a canonical key; the model cannot guarantee consistent spelling across separate calls, and downstream manual fixes multiply.

quiz.q: An extraction pipeline produces a category that must be one of 40 fixed values, but some rows contain invented categories. What should be added?
choices: Constrain the output to an enumeration of the 40 values and route non-matching results to review
A longer prompt that repeats the list of categories several times to emphasise the allowed values
A larger model, since stronger models are less likely to invent new category names
A nightly job that maps every unknown category to the closest-sounding allowed one automatically
quiz.explain: An enumeration constrains the output and validation routes the rest to review; repetition or bigger models reduce but do not prevent invention, and silent remapping hides errors.

days.recap: Run batch AI with typed, enumerated schemas, vision models for images and scans, validation of content as well as shape, and review routing for anything that fails.

days.title: Provenance, South or North of the Ontology, and Code Repositories

concepts.heading: Preserving Prompts and Raw Responses
concepts.body: Every AI-generated value that may need explaining later should be stored with the prompt version, the model identifier and the raw model response that produced it. With these, a wrong label can be traced to the prompt, the model or the parsing, that stage fixed, the case added to the suite, and exactly the affected rows reprocessed. Templates are stored once per version and only the per-row injected variables are kept with each output, so any prompt can be reconstructed. Writing prompt version and model id as columns on every enriched row makes provenance queryable and lets backfills target a specific version.

concepts.heading: Retention and Reproducibility
concepts.body: Keep cheap audit metadata such as prompt version, model id and input reference on every row, and keep raw responses under a documented retention window plus a sample. Re-running a model may not give the same answer, so the stored response is the record, and that limit of reproducibility should be documented. Storing the inputs and the prompt recipe per record still allows processing to be re-run and compared on a different model. For consequential decisions, also store the model's structured reason and an input snapshot reference, and for extracted values an evidence span validated against the document.

concepts.heading: South or North of the Ontology
concepts.body: The Ontology is the semantic layer between data pipelines and applications. Work south of it runs in pipelines and publishes results as object properties: compute once, validate, store, reuse. Work north of it runs at interaction time in functions, agents and apps, using the current user, selection and moment. Choose by consumer breadth, freshness, reusability, scale and cost: content-only results needed by many consumers, or values used to sort and filter across many objects, go south; drafting a reply to the email a user is reading goes north.

concepts.heading: Combining the Layers
concepts.body: Many workflows use both layers. Precompute stable features and candidate actions in a pipeline, then generate the final recommendation on demand with the live context. A per-item AI result that has become a shared need, such as an email class used by several reports, moves south into an event-driven or batch step that stores it on arrival. Generate outputs when and where they are consumed: on object creation through an automation, or on first open with a short cache, keeping batch generation for universal needs.

concepts.heading: Code Repositories for Programmatic Batch AI
concepts.body: Scheduled, rate-limited, retried or library-dependent AI processing belongs in a Code Repositories transform. Control the call rate in code with client-side limits under the provider's limit, bounded concurrency, batching where supported and backoff on throttling. Handle errors per row: catch the exception, record the row with a failure status and message, continue, and reprocess only failed rows in a follow-up run while monitoring the failure rate. Checkpointing lets a job resume after interruptions or known provider maintenance, and outputs can be cached by input content and prompt version so only changed records are regenerated.

examPoints: When a scenario needs an AI result on every object for sorting, filtering or many consumers, prefer computing it south of the Ontology in a pipeline and storing it as a property; when it depends on the current user's context, prefer north at interaction time.

When a scenario shows a batch AI job failing as a whole because of throttling or a few bad rows, prefer rate limiting, backoff and per-row error handling with recorded retries in a Code Repositories transform.

quiz.q: A sentiment score must be shown and sortable on every customer object in several apps. Where should it be computed?
choices: North of the Ontology, in a Logic function called each time a user opens a customer
In an agent that users ask for the score whenever they need to sort the list
South of the Ontology, in a pipeline step that stores the score as a property on each object
In each app separately, so that every team can tune its own prompt for the score
quiz.explain: Values used to sort or filter across many objects and needed by many consumers must be materialized by the pipeline; on-view computation cannot sort, and per-app copies diverge.

quiz.q: An audit asks why a record was labelled high risk six months ago. Which stored data makes this answerable?
choices: Only the final label, since the model can be asked today to explain why it would choose that label
A screenshot of the dashboard taken on the day the label was produced
The current prompt template, because prompts rarely change after a pipeline is published
The prompt version, model identifier, input reference and raw response stored with the label
quiz.explain: Provenance stored with each AI value lets you reconstruct what the model received and returned; asking the model now gives a new answer, and the current template may differ from the one used.

days.recap: Store prompt version, model id, inputs and raw responses with AI outputs, place work south or north of the Ontology by consumers and context, and use Code Repositories for rate-limited, per-row-resilient batch jobs.

days.title: Evaluation Suites, Evaluators and Metrics

concepts.heading: Anatomy of an Evaluation Suite
concepts.body: An evaluation suite has test cases, a target function or agent, evaluators and metrics. Each test case has an input, an expected result and an evaluator that compares the two. Cases come from representative real inputs spanning types, formats and tricky phrasings, and expected outputs are confirmed independently, never taken from the function under test. A suite is only as useful as its coverage: a few hundred well-chosen cases with deliberately hard ones tell you more than thousands of clean samples.

concepts.heading: Deterministic Evaluators First
concepts.body: Use deterministic evaluators for deterministic outputs: exact match for identifiers, dates and amounts, a tolerance only where rounding is legitimate, set comparison for unordered lists, and checks such as length limits or citations that must match retrieved chunks. Structured outputs are evaluated per field according to each field's meaning and aggregated into a case score, with per-field results kept so you can see which field failed. Even for free text, factual anchors such as a stated reason that must match the record can be checked deterministically. Building one evaluator per requirement, and making it deterministic wherever the requirement allows, keeps scores stable from run to run.

concepts.heading: Model-Graded Evaluation for Free Text
concepts.body: Model graders scale evaluation of free text, but they need explicit criteria, calibration against human ratings and handling of their own non-determinism. Grade with a per-criterion rubric covering required facts, absence of fabricated content, forbidden content, tone and length, rather than similarity to a single reference answer. Watch for grader bias, such as favouring longer answers, and correct it with explicit content criteria, a length-neutral instruction and calibration with short correct answers. When a grader is changed, the score scale changes too, so recalibrate and re-baseline before comparing.

concepts.heading: Groundedness and Tool Selection
concepts.body: Correctness and groundedness are different measures: an answer can sound right without being supported by the retrieved context. A groundedness evaluator checks each claim against the passages provided, and it is most reliable when claim-level and calibrated against humans. For agents, evaluate tool selection explicitly by comparing the tools called, and their arguments, with the expected calls for each case, including cases where no tool should be used. Final-answer accuracy alone hides an agent that reached the right answer through the wrong tool.

concepts.heading: Reporting Metrics Separately
concepts.body: A useful evaluation reports correctness, groundedness, retrieval hit rate, refusal behaviour, latency and cost as separate figures. A headline score can summarize them, but its components should be visible beneath it with release gates per component, so one strong number cannot mask a regression elsewhere. When comparing prompt or model variants, run them on the same fixed suite with the same model settings and evaluators, repeated to estimate variance, and look at per-case results as well as averages. Judge an AI feature by these quality figures together with its cost and measured outcomes, trended over time.

examPoints: When a scenario asks how to evaluate an output with a single correct value, prefer a deterministic evaluator such as exact match over a model grader.
When a scenario shows a fluent answer that the retrieved context does not support, prefer a groundedness evaluator that checks claims against the context over a correctness or style score.

quiz.q: A function extracts an invoice number and a total. Which evaluator design is most appropriate for these two fields?
choices: Exact match on the invoice number and a numeric comparison on the total, with tolerance only for legitimate rounding
A model grader asked to rate from one to ten how plausible the extracted values look
A similarity score between the extracted values and the full text of the invoice
A human review of every case each time the function changes, with no automated checks
quiz.explain: Deterministic outputs deserve deterministic evaluators; plausibility ratings and text similarity cannot confirm an exact value, and reviewing everything by hand does not scale.

quiz.q: A model grader consistently gives higher scores to longer answers even when shorter ones are correct. What should be done?
choices: Instruct the function under test to write longer answers so they score better
Replace the grader with a larger model and keep the existing scores as the baseline
Remove free-text evaluation and judge the function only on latency and cost
Add explicit content criteria and a length-neutral instruction, calibrate with short correct answers, then re-baseline
quiz.explain: Grader bias is corrected through explicit criteria and human calibration, followed by a new baseline; gaming the grader or dropping quality measurement hides the problem.

days.recap: Build suites from representative cases with independently confirmed expectations, use deterministic evaluators wherever possible and calibrated rubrics for free text, and report each metric separately.

days.title: Edge Cases, Regression Versus Variance, and Feedback Loops

concepts.heading: Edge, Adversarial and High-Consequence Cases
concepts.body: Prioritize cases that could produce the worst outcomes: inputs just past a threshold, violations hidden in descriptions, users without the right to request something, and large ambiguous requests. For agents that act, include cases where the correct behaviour is to execute, to refuse, to escalate and to ignore injected instructions, and check the resulting object state, not just the reply. Destructive bulk requests should be tested with cases that expect a scope summary, a confirmation request and no change. Edge cases also come from the domain's hard spots, such as time-zone transitions or unsatisfiable constraints, with defined expected behaviour.

concepts.heading: Measuring Refusal Both Ways
concepts.body: Refusal behaviour is measured explicitly with cases that expect a refusal or escalation and cases where refusing would be wrong. Unanswerable cases are built from verified gaps in the corpus, expecting an explicit 'not found' and scoring the absence of invented content. Unauthorized requests are tested across identity, role and impersonation, including spoofed authority in the text, asserting that nothing is approved. Indirect injection is tested with documents that contain instructions, asserting that the content is treated as data and no Action results.

concepts.heading: Regression or Variance
concepts.body: Model outputs vary from run to run, so a small score change may be noise. Before calling a regression, run both versions several times on the same unchanged suite, estimate the spread, and inspect which cases flip and why. Set thresholds relative to measured variance and reduce variance where possible, for example with lower temperature or a larger suite. Never change the suite and the function in the same comparison: measure original and new cases separately to tell distribution shift from regression. A comparison is reproducible only if suite version, grader, model configuration and parameters are the same.

concepts.heading: Segment, Version and Tier the Suite
concepts.body: Averages hide localized damage, so segment results by category and consequence and weight decisions by the segments that matter. Version the suite and review changes to expected answers like code, since an incorrect edit to expected values looks exactly like a regression. Large suites are tiered: a fast stratified subset with repeats on every change during development, and the full suite nightly and before release. Suites are curated for coverage, not size: deduplicate near-identical cases, keep a stratified core, and admit new cases that cover new failure types.

concepts.heading: Feedback Loops and Drift
concepts.body: User feedback and human corrections are signals to test against, not controls to react to blindly. Capture the original output, the edited or overturned result, a structured reason and the input reference, verify a sample as true failures, convert confirmed cases into evaluation cases, and prioritize fixes by frequency and impact. If suite scores stay stable while production metrics worsen, production inputs have drifted, so refresh the suite with recent production cases. Guard release gates against overfitting to the suite with held-out, rotating cases and production metrics.

examPoints: When a scenario reports a small score drop after a change, prefer repeated runs on a fixed suite and per-case inspection to establish variance before calling it a regression or rolling back.

When a scenario describes thumbs-down feedback or human overturns, prefer reviewing them, converting confirmed failures into evaluation cases and prioritizing fixes over directly retuning prompts on each complaint.

quiz.q: A team added 50 hard cases to its suite and changed the prompt in the same week; the overall score fell from 94% to 88%. What is the correct reading?
choices: The prompt change caused a regression and should be rolled back immediately
The new cases are wrong and should be removed so the score returns to its earlier level
The suite's distribution changed, so original and new cases must be scored separately to see what the prompt did
The grader became stricter, so the scores should simply be adjusted upward by six points
quiz.explain: Changing the suite and the function together makes the comparison meaningless; scoring the original cases separately shows whether the prompt regressed and what the new cases reveal.

quiz.q: Which test best checks an agent's resistance to indirect prompt injection?
choices: A user politely asking the agent to summarize a normal supplier document
A document containing an embedded instruction to approve an invoice, expecting a summary with no Action taken
A request with spelling mistakes to check that the agent still understands the question
A long conversation that checks whether the agent remembers the user's earlier messages
quiz.explain: Indirect injection hides instructions in content the agent processes; the test asserts the content is treated as data and that no Action or state change results.

days.recap: Test the worst-case, refusal and injection paths explicitly, establish variance before declaring regressions, version and tier the suite, and turn verified feedback into new cases.

days.title: Automate Triggers, Effects and Function-Backed Actions

concepts.heading: Triggers and Effects
concepts.body: Automate watches the Ontology for conditions and runs effects when they occur. Triggers include object creation, property changes and schedules; effects include running functions, applying Actions and sending notifications. A requirement shaped like 'when a complaint is created, classify it and alert a manager if it is urgent' maps to a creation trigger, a function effect and a conditional notification effect. Event triggers suit per-item work and scheduled triggers suit periodic aggregates such as a nightly summary or a weekly digest.

concepts.heading: Precise Trigger Conditions
concepts.body: Trigger on the properties or transitions that matter rather than on any change. 'When a document moves from draft to submitted' is a property-change trigger conditioned on the old and new values, scoped per object. AI steps should start when data is ready, for example when required fields are present, not simply when the object is created, with a fallback sweep for anything missed. Business rules such as 'never contact a do-not-contact customer' and 'send only once' belong in conditions, with state recorded on the object so 'once' can be checked.

concepts.heading: Avoiding Self-Triggering Loops
concepts.body: An automation must not satisfy its own trigger. If a function's write changes a property the trigger watches, each run starts the next one. Narrow the trigger to specific status transitions, keep what the automation writes separate from what it watches, add a loop guard, and verify with run counts before and after the change. Gating on explicit dependency status, such as a migration-complete flag, is safer than relying on timing assumptions.

concepts.heading: Function-Backed Actions
concepts.body: A plain Action applies edits defined declaratively. A function-backed Action runs code, which may call an AI function, to compute the edits at execution time, for example generating a summary and writing it with validation. Use function-backed Actions when the edit must be computed or depends on conditional logic across objects, and keep simple edits declarative. In an automation, a function effect can produce AI content and an Action effect can then create or change the object, such as a review task carrying the drafted summary.

concepts.heading: Matching Execution to the Workload
concepts.body: Choose the trigger and execution style that fits the work. A daily feed is processed once when it has landed, as a set, rather than as thousands of per-object runs. High-volume AI automations are paced against provider limits with batched, rate-limited execution, retrying failed items within the same window. Time-bound per-object processing should write an auditable result object and raise an alert if any object lacks a result after a deadline. Workflows branch by consequence: the routine path runs automatically and the sensitive path waits for human approval.

examPoints: When a scenario shows an automation firing repeatedly on the same object after it writes back, prefer narrowing the trigger to specific transitions and separating written properties from watched ones over adding delays.
When a scenario requires an Ontology edit whose values must be computed, possibly by AI, at execution time, prefer a function-backed Action over a declarative Action or a direct write.

quiz.q: Each new support email must be classified on arrival, and managers want one summary of the day's emails every evening. Which setup fits?
choices: An object-creation trigger for per-email classification and a separate nightly scheduled trigger for the summary
A single scheduled trigger every five minutes that reclassifies all emails and rebuilds the summary
One creation trigger that classifies each email and also regenerates the full daily summary every time
No automation, with users running the classification function by hand whenever they open an email
quiz.explain: Event triggers suit per-item work and scheduled triggers suit periodic aggregates; polling reprocesses everything, rebuilding the summary per email wastes calls, and manual runs leave emails unclassified.

quiz.q: A user's button click should generate a summary with an AI function and save it on the case. How should the write happen?
choices: The function writes the summary straight into the module's display state without any Action
The user copies the generated text and pastes it into the case property by hand
A function-backed Action calls the function and writes the summary to the case under the Action's rules
An automation polls every case each minute and writes a new summary whether or not anything changed
quiz.explain: Writes from an app go through a function-backed Action, which computes the value at execution time and applies the edit under the Action's permissions and validation; display state is not a saved write, and polling wastes calls.

days.recap: Map 'when X, do Y' to Automate triggers and effects, trigger on the exact transitions that matter without self-triggering, and use function-backed Actions for computed edits.

days.title: Chaining AI Steps, Retries, Idempotency and Safe Changes to Live Workflows

concepts.heading: AI Recommends, Actions Execute
concepts.body: Chain AI output through validation into an Action; the model never writes before its output has been checked. A Logic function returns typed details or a recommendation, validation runs, and a function-backed Action applies the change under business rules, with an approval task gating the high-consequence path, such as discounts above a threshold. Implement the AI logic once as a published function and expose it through an Action for users and as an effect for automations, so both share one version. Keep the Action's validation as the final guard even when the function already clamps or rejects out-of-range values.

concepts.heading: No Silent Nulls Between Steps
concepts.body: When a step fails, it should return an explicit error state and route the item to retry or review rather than passing an empty value to the next step. Validate outputs inside the function, fail loudly instead of writing empties, and monitor written properties, for example with an alert on the rate of empty values. A required input that is missing should cause a failure, not a silent default. Step-level records on a linked run record, holding the step, function version, input and output references, status and timestamp, make each run traceable and reproducible.

concepts.heading: Long AI Work Runs Asynchronously
concepts.body: Actions should stay fast. For long AI work started from Workshop, the button applies an Action that records a request object and returns; an automation picks up the request, runs the AI call, writes the result and status to the object, and notifies the user. The module shows the status from the object, so the user is never left with a blocked session. AI results that others rely on are persisted through Actions that also record the generator, timestamp and version.

concepts.heading: Retries and Idempotency
concepts.body: When a workflow can retry, every write must be idempotent so a repeated run cannot duplicate its effect. Key each created record to its source, such as one payment request per invoice, and check for an existing one first; guard external sends with a per-event delivery marker; and give external calls an idempotency key. Record each step's state on the object so a retry resumes from the failed step only. In Automate, retries can be configured on Action and Logic effects and fallback effects exist, but the order of multiple Action effects is not guaranteed, so decisions that depend on order must enforce it in your own logic.

concepts.heading: Changing a Live Automation Safely
concepts.body: Before turning on a live automation, run it on representative objects, including edge cases, and inspect every result. Rehearse multi-step chains in isolation, on a branch or with test objects and effects pointed at non-production targets, then enable with limited scope. Ship changes as a new tested function version and switch at a quiet moment while in-flight runs finish on the old one, with monitoring and rollback ready. Protect consequential automated changes with Action validation, volume limits and anomaly alerts. Backfills run separately as bounded, resumable, rate-limited batches with idempotent writes.

examPoints: When a scenario shows duplicate records or messages after an automation retried, prefer idempotent writes keyed to the source plus per-event markers over disabling retries.

When a scenario changes the function behind a live automation, prefer a new evaluated version tested on representative objects and switched over with monitoring and rollback over editing the live version in place.

quiz.q: An automation retries when a downstream service times out, and some invoices now have two payment requests. What should be fixed?
choices: Disable retries on the automation so that a timeout never causes a second attempt
Add an instruction to the AI function telling it not to create duplicate payment requests
Run a weekly clean-up job that deletes the newer of any two payment requests per invoice
Make the Action idempotent by keying each payment request to its invoice and checking for an existing one first
quiz.explain: With retries, every write must be idempotent so a repeated run cannot add a second record; disabling retries loses work, prompts cannot enforce uniqueness, and clean-up jobs act after the damage.

quiz.q: An analysis started from a Workshop button takes several minutes and users see the session hang. What is the better design?
choices: Raise the Action's timeout so that the button waits until the analysis has finished
An Action that records a request, an automation that runs the analysis and writes result and status, and a status view in the module
Ask users to keep the module open and avoid clicking anything else until the analysis returns
Split the analysis across three buttons that users press one after another in the right order
quiz.explain: Long AI work runs asynchronously: the Action stays fast, an automation does the work, and the object carries status for the module and notifications; longer timeouts or manual sequences keep the session blocked.

days.recap: Chain AI output through validation into Actions, make failures explicit, run long work asynchronously, make every retried write idempotent, and change live automations only through tested versions.

days.title: Model Selection, Multi-Provider Resilience and BYOM

concepts.heading: Requirements First, Then the Smallest Model That Passes
concepts.body: Select models from the task's requirements. First filter by hard constraints: required capability such as reading images, data residency, and latency for interactive use. Among the models that remain, pick the smallest or cheapest one that meets the accuracy requirement on the evaluation suite, then confirm throughput and cost at the expected volume. A larger model is justified only when the task's requirement needs the measured gain; when quality is met and latency does not matter, as in a nightly batch, cost decides.

concepts.heading: When Bigger or Specialized Models Are Right
concepts.body: Premium models are the right choice when the task is high-value, low-volume or needs a long context window that chunking cannot replace, for example reasoning across long documents with cross-references, and evaluation confirms the gain. Multilingual work needs a model that meets the requirement in every language, verified with a language-stratified suite weighted by the real language mix rather than by headline benchmarks. A routing design can escalate to a stronger model on evidence, such as low confidence, a failed validation or a known high-consequence request type, rather than using it for everything. Whatever the choice, record the evidence behind it and revisit it when models or volumes change.

concepts.heading: Multi-Provider Resilience
concepts.body: A single provider is a single point of failure. Configure a fallback to a comparable model from another provider before an outage, evaluate it with the suite so its quality, groundedness and refusal behaviour are known, and confirm it meets the same residency and budget rules. Make every request's model visible in observability. Exercise the fallback path regularly with drills or a small share of traffic, and keep its prompts and evaluations current, since an untested fallback may fail when it is needed.

concepts.heading: BYOM and Custom Endpoints
concepts.body: When a model must be self-hosted or self-licensed, for example to run inside the organization's own environment or because the organization licensed a model the catalog does not offer, register it through bring-your-own-model or a custom endpoint. AIP Logic, agents and pipelines then call it through the platform with the platform's permissions, observability and governance applied. Calling a model directly from outside the platform, or testing new models with personal keys or exported data, bypasses those controls. New models are evaluated through governed enablement in a test scope.

concepts.heading: Pinning, Deprecations and Migrations
concepts.body: Pin model versions for stability and record retirement dates. Treat a deprecation as a planned migration: select the successor early, run the evaluation suite, adjust prompts, and roll out as a versioned change with rollback, keeping the model change visible in observability. Adopting any new model follows the same path: confirm enablement and compliance, evaluate against the incumbent, check prompt differences and roll out gradually. Organizations usually standardize on a small evaluated portfolio of models with per-workflow selection and fallbacks rather than a single model for every task.

examPoints: When a scenario offers a larger model to fix a task that a smaller one already passes, prefer the smallest model that meets the requirement on the evaluation suite, confirmed against cost and throughput.

When a scenario requires a self-hosted or self-licensed model, prefer registering it through BYOM or a custom endpoint so it stays under platform governance, rather than calling it from outside the platform.

quiz.q: Two models both pass the quality threshold for a nightly classification batch; one costs a third as much and is slower. Which should be chosen?
choices: The faster, more expensive model, because lower latency always improves batch quality
The cheaper model, since quality is met and latency does not matter for a nightly batch
Both models on alternating nights, so that their results can be compared indefinitely
Neither; the team should wait for a newer model that is both cheaper and faster
quiz.explain: With quality met and latency irrelevant, cost is the remaining differentiator; record the decision and revisit it later.

quiz.q: A provider has announced that the model version a workflow is pinned to will retire in four months. What is the best plan?
choices: Wait until the retirement date and then switch to whichever replacement the provider offers at that time
Switch to the newest model today without evaluation, since newer models are generally better
Remove the pin now so that the workflow always follows the provider's latest release
Select a successor now, run the suite, adjust prompts, and roll out as a versioned change with rollback
quiz.explain: Deprecations are planned migrations with evaluation, versioning and observability; waiting or switching blindly leaves quality unknown, and unpinning invites unannounced behaviour changes.

days.recap: Choose models by hard constraints first and then the smallest one that passes evaluation, keep a tested fallback on a second provider, bring own models in through BYOM or custom endpoints, and migrate pinned versions deliberately.

days.title: Observability, Latency and Cost Optimization

concepts.heading: Traces and Telemetry Come First
concepts.body: When a live AI system drifts, slows down or costs more, start from traces and telemetry. AIP Observability and execution history record each run's status, duration, tokens and model, and session traces record each stage's inputs, outputs, tool calls and timing. Comparing two versions stage by stage on the same inputs shows which stage changed. Every production run should carry a surfaced request id so an intermittent failure reported by a user can be pulled and replayed.

concepts.heading: Reading Latency and Errors
concepts.body: Averages hide the tail, so monitor p95 and p99 latency and break slow requests down by step and input size. Rising timeouts are a trend to diagnose: find in the traces which stage grew, correlate it with inputs or dependencies, fix that stage and define a timeout with fallback behaviour. A context-length error means some input, such as retrieved context, history or a document, grew beyond budget; find it in the trace, bound it and add a pre-flight check. After a release, alert on error-rate thresholds and on deviation from the pre-release baseline.

concepts.heading: Attributing Cost
concepts.body: Decompose cost into volume and per-request size, and investigate whichever moved. A volume increase points to a new consumer, retries, a loop or growth; spikes in windows when users are not active point to automations, backfills or retry loops, visible in execution history by caller. Per-request growth is tracked by trending tokens per request with a drift alert. Output tokens matter too: a model version change or instruction drift can make outputs verbose, which schemas, maximum token limits and length alerts constrain.

concepts.heading: Cutting Latency Without Losing Quality
concepts.body: Profile the trace before reaching for a different model. Run independent retrievals and tool calls in parallel, so the wait is the longest single call, with timeouts and fallbacks. Pass only relevant chunks, replace model-based validation with deterministic checks, remove redundant calls and merge steps only where the suite shows no loss. Long work belongs in an asynchronous flow with progress and notification instead of a blocking session. Slowly changing external data can be refreshed into the Ontology on a schedule so requests read a local copy.

concepts.heading: Cutting Cost in the Right Order
concepts.body: Measure the cost breakdown first. Then remove waste, such as oversized context or an extra checking call that does not improve outcomes, add caching, route easy cases to a cheaper model, and change the main model last, re-evaluating at each step. Cache answers only for recurring, context-independent questions, keyed on the normalized question and the content version, with invalidation; within a session, retrieval results can be reused until the topic changes. Prompt techniques such as few-shot examples are judged by their measured quality gain against their token cost. Observability itself has a cost, so sample full traces while keeping all errors and cheap metrics on every request.

examPoints: When a scenario reports slow or costly AI runs, prefer analysing traces to parallelize independent steps and remove oversized context or redundant calls before switching models.
When a scenario shows a cost spike, prefer separating volume from per-request size and attributing calls by caller and time, which often reveals an automation, backfill or retry loop.

quiz.q: An agent's turn makes four independent lookups one after another before calling the model, and users find it slow. What should be done first?
choices: Run the four lookups in parallel with timeouts and fallbacks, so the wait is the longest single call
Switch to a larger model, which will reason faster over the results of the four lookups
Remove two of the lookups at random to halve the time spent before the model call
Add a progress message and keep the lookups sequential, since order may matter to the model
quiz.explain: Independent calls can run in parallel, cutting pre-prompt time to the slowest one; a larger model is usually slower, and dropping lookups at random harms answers.

quiz.q: A workflow's monthly AI cost doubled while tokens per request stayed flat, and the extra calls appear overnight when no users are active. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model provider raised its prices, so every request now costs twice as much
Prompts became longer after a recent edit, raising the cost of each request
Users started asking more complex questions during the working day
Automated runs such as a nightly automation, a backfill or a retry loop are adding volume
quiz.explain: Flat per-request size means the increase is volume; calls in non-user windows point to automations, backfills or retries, visible in execution history by caller.

days.recap: Diagnose from traces and telemetry, watch tail latency and tokens per request, attribute cost to volume or size and to its caller, and optimize by parallelizing, trimming, caching and routing before changing models.

days.title: Execution Identity, Platform Controls, Audit and Sensitive Data

concepts.heading: Execution Identity
concepts.body: A function can run as the invoking user, so its results reflect what that user may see, or as a configured identity for a controlled, elevated task. Retrieval and user-facing answers run as the user. A narrow elevated operation, such as returning a safe aggregate over marked data, runs under a least-privilege service identity with restricted invocation, validated output shape and audited runs that record the triggering user. Agent tools executed as the user let Ontology permissions decide what each person sees, so an unauthorized user gets an empty result the agent can explain.

concepts.heading: Why It Works for the Author but Not in Automation
concepts.body: Automate evaluates conditions and runs Action and Logic effects as the automation's owner, while notification effects use each recipient's permissions. A function that works when its author runs it can therefore fail in an automation because a different principal lacks access to the objects or tools involved. Diagnose by identifying the principal and what it cannot reach, then grant specific least-privilege access or change the execution mode deliberately. Widening access for everyone to make an error disappear is never the answer.

concepts.heading: Platform Controls: Enrollment, Georestrictions and Capacity
concepts.body: Models and AI capabilities are enabled per enrollment by administrators, who review policy, cost and data handling; a team that needs a model requests it rather than bypassing the process. Enabling only approved models enforces provider policy, because workflows can then select only compliant ones. Model calls are data flows, so data residency is enforced through model enablement and georestrictions and verified in traces. Capacity and spend controls such as quotas, rate limits and budget alerts bound usage and should fail safe; a throttled workflow is optimized and given a justified, monitored increase rather than having limits removed.

concepts.heading: Audit Evidence and Provenance
concepts.body: Audit evidence for an AI-driven decision comes from stored inputs, retrieved context, model and prompt versions and the run trace, plus Action logs that record who approved a change, not from the model's own narrative. Record prompt, model and workflow versions with a trace reference on every AI-produced object. Lineage from a generated deliverable back to its sources, with their versions and approval status, shows what it was built from. Demonstrating that an agent did not access a dataset relies on configuration history, permission records for its execution identities and access logs.

concepts.heading: Sensitive Data in AI Workflows
concepts.body: Mask sensitive identifiers deterministically before text reaches a model, and govern AI outputs with the same markings as their inputs. Markings are mandatory and propagate through transform and analysis logic, so summaries derived from marked documents carry the marking, or the workflow excludes those documents from broad-audience outputs. A retrieval corpus of personal data needs minimization, redaction, inherited access controls on chunks and a restricted audience. Traces and observability data inherit the sensitivity of what they contain. Every derived artefact, from chunks and vectors to raw responses, should trace to its source record so deletion can be executed and verified.

examPoints: When a scenario shows a function succeeding for its author but failing in an automation, prefer checking the execution identity the automation runs as and granting that principal least-privilege access.

When a scenario requires data residency or spend limits, prefer platform configuration such as model enablement, georestrictions and capacity controls over prompt instructions or after-the-fact reports.

quiz.q: A search function used by an agent should return only the records each employee is allowed to see. How should it run?
choices: As a service identity with broad read access, with the prompt telling the agent which records to hide
As the invoking user, so Ontology permissions decide what each person can see
